papers.title: IndicTalk
papers.summary: 1,328,604 event-grounded multi-turn conversations, 18 language varieties, 9 Indic languages, code-mixed in both native-script and Romanized forms; built via news-grounding + persona-conditioned generation + automatic quality validation. Directly serves the project's stated #1 task (conversation); nothing else at this scale exists for Indic code-mixed dialogue. The paper says 'we will release' — verify the data is actually up before planning around it.

papers.title: Indic DiarBench
papers.summary: ~108 hours across all 22 scheduled languages with human-corrected, time-aligned, speaker-attributed transcriptions; near-field meetings, far-field and in-the-wild, capturing code-mixing, dialect and speaker overlap. First joint diarization+ASR benchmark covering all 22 languages. Open access — add to the EVAL suite.

papers.title: BHARATI
papers.summary: Morphology-aware SentencePiece BPE tokenizers on a 781MB balanced corpus across seven languages, handling Sanskrit/Tamil agglutination and sandhi. Achieves 2.6 tokens per Indian Knowledge System technical term vs 5.25 for GPT-2 and ~90% sequence-length reduction vs GPT-2/byte-level on a released 490-sentence IKS test set, with the measurement script published.

papers.title: The Tokenizer Tax
papers.summary: Measured on FLORES-200 across six tokenizers and fourteen Indian languages: an average 8.0x tokenization tax under cl100k_base (13.0x for Malayalam), effective context window cut to as little as 12%, mechanism identified as failed byte-pair merges (Pearson r = 0.89), and XLM-R/o200k_base reducing the average Indic tax by 73%. Quantifies and validates the main document's claim that the tokenizer decision is worth more than 2T extra tokens; elevates it from workstream to gating milestone.

papers.title: Can OCR-VLMs Read Devanagari? A Stress-Test Benchmark and Post-Correction Study
papers.summary: Ten systems benchmarked on Hindi/Devanagari across four synthetic degradations and 300 real printed scans. On clean rendered text all ten cluster at chrF++ 91-98; on real scans nine of ten collapse across a 76-point range. EasyOCR falls 93.6 -> 58.3, GPT-5.5 drops to 58.5, and olmOCR-7B falls to 40.5 — worst in class. Qwen3-VL-8B wins among open models at 75.2 on a single 24 GB GPU; DeepSeek-OCR has the best median but rare catastrophic repetition failures (up to 71x reference length). Reverses the main document's 'fine-tune olmOCR for Indic' recommendation.

papers.title: Conversational IndicTrans2 adaptation
papers.summary: Adapts IndicTrans2-1B to conversational register across all 21 Indic languages using only public data (OpenSubtitles, BPCC-H-Daily, Tatoeba) via experience replay + model souping: +6.2 mean conversational chrF with no FLORES regression. Directly reusable recipe. The authors' own blind human + multi-model check did not confirm a perceived quality improvement — they call it register matching, not better translation; the document says adopt the technique and the scepticism.

papers.title: SCRIBE
papers.summary: Diagnostic evaluation plus rich transcription models for Indic ASR. Useful for the ASR-transcription pipeline of Section 8.

papers.title: IndicKLAR
papers.summary: Cross-lingual knowledge consistency, code-mixed vs native, across nine open-weight models: the native-language accuracy gap to English reaches ~0.50, but code-mixed inputs close most of it — to within ~0.05 of English — with no model-level intervention. Strategically important: suggests code-mixed input is a far more efficient path to Indic parity than native-script-only training, and should influence the data mixture.

papers.title: AgriGov
papers.summary: Structured multilingual dataset of Indian government farmer schemes. Domain-specific; matches BharatGen's agriculture vertical.

papers.title: Darshana Graph
papers.summary: Parallel commentary corpus for comparative Indian philosophy. Rare classical/Indian Knowledge System content.

papers.title: BhashaSutra
papers.summary: Task-centric unified survey of Indian NLP datasets. The document recommends using it as the master index — 'the most complete catalogue in existence'. Date given only as 'Apr 2026' in Addendum A.4 (and as '2026' in the Section 20 source index), with no day, so the date field is null.

papers.title: DataOrchestra: Learning to Orchestrate Per-Example Curation of Pretraining Data
papers.summary: The successor research line to OPUS-style selection, but for per-example processing: an orchestrator decides drop/keep/clean per chunk, then selects operations from programmatic edits to LLM rewriting with a generated instruction per rewrite. Validated by from-scratch pretrains at 0.5B-7B with stable average gains across 11 benchmarks, and effective for math continued-pretraining. To be read before finalizing the Section 17 pipeline — it is the strongest current argument that per-example adaptivity pays at the cleaning stage rather than the selection stage.

papers.title: IKS-Instruct
papers.summary: 24,795 instruction pairs across 7 languages (en/hi/sa/ta/te/kn/ml), 41 Vedic pedagogical techniques, aligned to CBSE classes 6-12; sources include the Bhagavad Gita, Thirukkural, Sangam literature, Vedic texts, Vedic-math sutra demonstrations, bilingual pairs and multi-turn dialogues. Fills two flagged gaps: BhashaBench's weakest domain (Ayurveda, GPT-4o 59.74%) and Section 10.1's proposed syllabus-structure curriculum-generation workaround, now executed by someone else. Licence unverified — check before ingestion.

papers.title: MoLGE: Mixture of Language-Group Experts
papers.summary: Dedicated experts per cluster of similar languages plus hierarchical LoRA for massively multilingual ASR, studying linguistic vs data-driven grouping criteria. Design evidence for MoE routing: converges from the ASR side with BharatGen's observation that MoE layers spontaneously grouped Hindi/Marathi and with Param-2's shared+routed expert split. Language-group experts (not per-language) are emerging as the pattern for 22-language capacity without dilution.

papers.title: The Physics of Multi-Turn Long-Horizon Planning
papers.summary: Controlled environment isolating how planning ability is acquired across pre- and post-training. Three findings for agentic data: explicit world-model construction via chain-of-thought state-transition data in pre-training yields stronger long-horizon generalization; atomic skills alone do not compose, but a little long-horizon data works; and suboptimal trajectories severely impair performance because errors amplify over horizons — so filter agentic traces hard rather than maximizing volume.

papers.title: XIH-Bench / Language Shapes Instruction-Hierarchy Compliance
papers.summary: Six languages, same- and cross-language instruction conflicts. Names a new failure mode — the 'Language Boundary Effect', where cross-language conflicts get higher compliance than same-language — and finds that language specialization makes lower-priority instructions in model-favored languages harder to override. Threat-model translation: an Indic-expert model acquires a jailbreak surface of injections written in its own favored languages, so cross-language-injection red-teaming joins the 22-language safety plan.

papers.title: PatiGonit22K
papers.summary: 22,441 Bengali math word problems, simple through multi-operation, translated/annotated/culturally adapted/verified. Corrects the report: Section 6 said Indic math/STEM is 'essentially absent'; amend to 'nearly absent' — this exists, though four orders of magnitude below MegaMath. The generate-and-translate strategy of Section 6 stands.

papers.title: Systematic analysis of LLM and transformer MT for English-Tamil across diverse data
papers.summary: Added to the Section 7 translation evidence base. The document records no further detail and issues no strategy change on the back of it.

risks.mitigation: Per-repo containers, 100-turn rollouts, harness co-development. Start the NeMo Gym work in parallel with data, not after.

risks.mitigation: §12.3, plus a fully held-out benchmark and a private eval set.

risks.mitigation: Use shared + routed experts (Param-2 uses 64 experts with 2 shared for code-mixing/domain-mixing) and monitor per-language expert utilisation from step one.
risks.note: §18.1. BharatGen reported MoE layers naturally grouping related languages (Hindi/Marathi). §B.5 adds MoLGE (arXiv:2607.24030) as converging evidence that language-*group* experts, not per-language experts, are the emerging pattern for 22-language capacity without dilution.

risks.mitigation: Keep the ✅ clean tier separable so you can retrain a compliant base if needed. Do not architect a corpus you cannot decompose.
risks.note: §18.2. The §18.2 table has no severity column, so the document assigns no severity; the section is titled "Legal and reputational risks" without labelling rows individually as legal or reputational. §14.1: the ruling is a single-judge interim order resting on a stretched Section 52(1)(a)(i), "one appeal away from re-examination".

risks.mitigation: Provenance index from day one; document-hash→shard→checkpoint lineage.

corrections.after: Do not use olmOCR for Devanagari. On 300 real printed Hindi/Devanagari scans, olmOCR-7B falls to 40.5 chrF++ — the worst-in-class result of ten systems, from the model behind olmOCR-Bench. Build the Indic OCR pipeline on Qwen3-VL-8B instead, the best open model at 75.2, which beats GPT-5.5 (58.5) and runs on a single 24 GB GPU. Strong English OCR does not predict Indic OCR. DeepSeek-OCR has the best median of any system but rare catastrophic repetition failures (outputs up to 71× reference length) destroy its mean. The addendum states the correction "is worth months of misdirected effort".

corrections.before: §1.3 listed tokenizer fertility as one of three things that will determine whether the model is good, asserted that "your tokenizer decision is worth more than 2T extra tokens", and told you to "budget a dedicated workstream". §18.1 rated it a High technical risk with the same workstream mitigation.
corrections.after: Elevate the tokenizer from a workstream to a gating milestone — nothing else should start until fertility is validated across all 22 scripts. The penalty is now measured: Indian languages pay an average 8.0× tokenization tax versus English under cl100k_base, reaching 13.0× for Malayalam, which reduces the effective context window to as little as 12% of what English users get for equivalent semantic content. The mechanism is identified and remediable — failed byte-pair merges leaving text fragmented into single-byte tokens, with merge failure correlating with tax at Pearson r = 0.89 — and XLM-R and o200k_base already reduce the average Indic tax by 73%.
corrections.why: The main document's #1 priority was an assertion; it is now backed by measurement on FLORES-200 across six tokenizers and fourteen Indian languages, with an identified mechanism. The finding also reframes the problem: "This is not a property of Indic scripts — it is a tokenizer design failure." §B.3 adds that because o200k already removes 73% of the tax, the retrofit path (BrahmicTokenizer-131K + Kronecker embeddings) starts closer to the goal than the main report assumed.
corrections.source: arXiv:2607.24276 — "The Tokenizer Tax", 27 July 2026; companion arXiv:2607.23319 — "BHARATI", 25 July 2026

corrections.before: §16 budgeted the corpus in unique tokens seen once: ~0.3T naturally-occurring Indic tokens exist, therefore natural Indic can only be ~2.0% of a 15T mix ("that ratio is uncomfortable and it is also unavoidable"), the 40–70% dedup loss is the single most likely schedule-breaker (§18.1), and the 20T milestone requires "aggressive multi-epoch reuse" left hand-waved.
corrections.after: Budget in unique pool × deliberate epoch schedule = effective tokens. ~0.3T unique natural Indic × 4 epochs ≈ 1.2T effective at roughly zero quality cost, with a theoretical ceiling of ~4.8T effective at 16× — raising the natural-Indic effective share from ~2% to ~7–8% without collecting a single new token. Two-to-four epochs on the highest-quality tiers (FineWeb-Edu, curated-clean) is cheap and standard. The dedup risk is half-defused: dedup down to the unique pool, then choose repetition deliberately, because dedup ≠ see-once. The 20T milestone becomes principled and quantified — ~11–13T unique plus a scheduled epoch plan concentrated on the scarce, high-value tiers.
corrections.why: The section-16 math was "Chinchilla-brained": it silently assumed every token is seen once. Muennighoff et al. measured that up to 4 epochs of repeated data is almost as good as fresh data — an 8.7B model trained 4 epochs on 44B unique tokens finished with only 0.5% higher validation loss than a single-epoch model on 178B unique tokens — with a decay constant R*_D ≈ 15, worthlessness at 40 epochs, a hard ceiling at U·(1+R*_D) ≈ 16× the unique pool, and an allocation rule that when data-constrained you scale epochs faster than parameters. Two honest limits attach: the measurements are English web data at ≤9B parameters, and nobody has measured R*_D for Indic, translated or synthetic text; and repetition works on whole tiers, not slivers (up-sampling 0.1% of a corpus 100× significantly degrades performance).
corrections.source: arXiv:2305.16264 — Muennighoff et al., "Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models" (in-project); arXiv:2401.00448 — Sardana & Frankle, cited at thesis level only

corrections.before: §17's pipeline treated the mixture as static and phase-scheduled (§16.3), and considered neither what a per-iteration data selector costs at scale nor what an English-trained quality classifier does to Indic data.
corrections.after: Static phase-scheduled mixing is confirmed as the production backbone — it is what the only in-project 120B run actually shipped with. Add an Always-ON lane: ~8% of every batch reserved for Tier-2/3 Indic scripts, agentic/world-model traces and benchmark training splits, bypassing every selector and quality classifier. Demote dynamic selection to ablation-stage tooling, never with an English-heavy reference proxy, and evaluate DataOrchestra for the *cleaning* stage instead of the selection stage.
corrections.why: LightningLM's golden proxy was English-heavy (cosine 0.876 with the English web band), so OPUS systematically under-valued Indic data and would have rejected it — "a single selector should not govern data whose value it cannot see". FineWeb-Edu-style quality classifiers carry exactly the same bias, so the Always-ON lane is the mechanism that guarantees Bodo, Santali, Dogri and Manipuri actually train at every stage. The economics also do not hold up: OPUS cost ~17% wall-clock throughput at the 5B stage in a sharded stack (30,429 vs 36,737 tok/s) against the 4.7% its own paper reports, and was disabled at 2B and again from 9B onward. The document marks this a 🔴 REVISION, though not one of the three labelled MATERIAL CORRECTIONs.
corrections.source: arXiv:2606.07404 — LightningLM 0.1V technical report (in-project); arXiv:2607.24717 — DataOrchestra, 28 July 2026

For calibration, Llama 4 trained on >30T tokens and Qwen3 on 36T across 119 languages — the 15T target is respectable but not frontier-scale, which is why the effective-token and growth machinery matter more than raw collection.

Nemotron-CC's authors found FineWebEdu-2 and DCLM held roughly 80% fuzzy duplicates because they only did sharded approximate dedup.

Section 18.1 rates 'global dedup collapses 23T to 9T, not 15T' as the single most likely schedule-breaker and prescribes running dedup on a 10% sample first. Synthesised data re-enters the same gate.

architectures.note: Read from the Hugging Face model card `sarvamai/sarvam-30b` (§A.1). Active params 2.4B non-embedding; 128 experts, top-6 routing, 1 shared expert; grouped KV (num_key_value_heads=4), 19 layers; intermediate 8192 / moe_intermediate 1024; rope_theta 8e6 with no RoPE scaling; auxiliary-loss-free router balancing, routed scaling factor 2.5; pre-trained on 16T tokens. params_total is taken from the model name and §A.6's 'Sarvam AI (30B, 105B)' - the Atlas never states a total-parameter figure. context is null: the card details rope_theta but no context length for the 30B. Positioning: 'reliable coding ability, best-in-class conversational quality across Indian languages'; handles multilingual voice calls while performing tool calls. Public rollout 6 March 2026.

LICENCE CORRECTED BY ADDENDUM A.1 ('MATERIAL CORRECTION #1 - Sarvam-105B is Apache 2.0, with full architecture disclosed'), read from the Hugging Face model card `sarvamai/sarvam-105b`; the addendum wins where it conflicts with Sections 1-21, which had treated Sarvam only as a reference point rather than 'a licence-free starting position'. 128 experts, top-8 routing, 1 shared expert; MLA-style attention with decoupled QK (q_head_dim 192 RoPE+noPE split, v_head_dim 128, head_dim 576, hidden_size 4096); FFN intermediate 16384 / moe_intermediate 2048; YaRN scaling factor 40 for 128K context; auxiliary-loss-free router balancing, routed scaling factor 2.5; pre-trained on 12T tokens. params_total from the model name and §A.6. Consequences per §A.1: it can be upcycled toward ~300B, used as an Indic teacher with zero licence-chain contamination (the clean alternative to BhashaKritika), and it sets the public bar any new 300B must beat.

§B.4, from the LightningLM 0.1V technical report (arXiv:2606.07404), described as in-project. A 120B sparse MoE: 460 routed experts, top-12 routing, 5.93B active (~5% of 118.67B stored), grown in four stages from a 1.78B dense seed (1.78B -> 5B -> 9B -> 120B), trained end-to-end on a single eight-GPU node; early stages at 4K context and 9B+ at 8K, so context here is the 8K final-stage figure. Capstone economics quoted as ~67 days and ~$100K-class without spot pricing for the V4 run. Corpus (§B.2): 1,118B tokens across 33,353 shards, ~1,254B effective, with a 78.1B always-ON tier at 8% of every batch and 31.3B dropped for contamination. Licence is null - the Atlas never states one.

BharatGen. Pre-trained on ~22T tokens (§1.1). §18.1: 'Param-2 uses 64 experts with 2 shared for code-mixing/domain-mixing', and BharatGen reported MoE layers naturally grouping related languages (Hindi/Marathi). Released under a BharatGen non-commercial licence (§3.6, §13.1) - §13.1 notes this blocks distillation-based data generation. params_total and params_active are read off the model name (17B total / A2.4B active); the Atlas states no separate figures. Context length is not stated. Trained on Bharat Data Sagar, which is not publicly redistributable.

Not a released model - a funded programme. §A.6, from Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw's written Lok Sabha reply of 22 July 2026: the government allocated ₹988.6 crore to the IIT Bombay-led BharatGen consortium specifically to develop a 1-trillion-parameter LLM, and BharatGen's own careers page states they are 'moving from 10B-class systems to 1 Trillion across language, document/vision, and speech'. §A.7 rates this MEDIUM confidence: 'government press coverage, not a tender document I read'. Active params, context and licence are all unstated. Strategic implication (§A.6): 'Your 300B sits between a free Apache-2.0 105B that already exists and a publicly-funded 1T that is being built.'

milestones.requirement: §16.2 'Stretch, phase 2': OCR of India's print archive at scale (an Indic-script OCR model), a BharatGen/Bharat Data Sagar data agreement, 2 epochs on the highest-quality 30% of the mix, and materially expanded synthetic generation. 'Do not plan the first training run around 20T' - reach it in a continued-pretraining phase. Addendum B.1 revises this from hand-waved to quantified: 20T processed ~= 11-13T unique plus a scheduled epoch plan concentrated on the scarce, high-value tiers (Muennighoff: up to 4 epochs is almost as good as fresh data; R*_D ~= 15).

legal.title: ANI v. OpenAI — first Indian judicial ruling on AI training
legal.detail: ANI (Asian News International) sued OpenAI in November 2024, alleging OpenAI used ANI's news reports without permission to train ChatGPT, and separately that ChatGPT fabricated stories attributed to ANI. The Digital News Publishers Association and the Federation of Indian Publishers intervened. The Delhi High Court refused the interim injunction; the suit continues to trial on the merits.
legal.status: interim — injunction refused, suit continues to trial
legal.action: Treat the outcome as favourable but provisional: build on it, do not bet the corpus architecture on it surviving trial or appeal.
legal.source: Delhi High Court, Justice Amit Bansal, judgment 24 July 2026, 135 pages (§14.1)
legal.note: §14 opens: "This section changed materially four days before this document was written." §A.7 grades the ruling high confidence — "multiple independent legal and business outlets" — and §20 lists the coverage as Business Standard, LawBeat, The New Publishing Standard. The document cites no case number or neutral citation.

legal.title: Training held prima facie fair dealing for research
legal.detail: OpenAI's storage and use of ANI's content to train its models is prima facie protected as "fair dealing" for "private or personal use, including research".
legal.status: prima facie finding at the interim-injunction stage
legal.action: You may rely on it as the current Indian position on ingestion for training, while keeping the corpus decomposable in case it is re-examined.
legal.source: Section 52(1)(a)(i) of the Copyright Act, 1957, as applied in ANI v. OpenAI, 24 July 2026 (§14.1)
legal.note: §14.1 also states this stretch of Section 52(1)(a)(i) "is the entire legal foundation" for training in India — see L12.

legal.title: ANI failed to establish memorisation or reproduction
legal.detail: ANI failed to establish that ChatGPT memorised or reproduced its copyrighted news reports.
legal.status: prima facie finding at the interim-injunction stage
legal.action: Run and document memorisation testing so you can affirmatively demonstrate low memorisation — see L26.
legal.source: ANI v. OpenAI, Delhi High Court, 24 July 2026 (§14.1)

legal.title: Copyright protects expression, not facts
legal.detail: Copyright protects expression, not the underlying facts or information — "news of the day" is not protected.
legal.status: prima facie finding at the interim-injunction stage
legal.source: ANI v. OpenAI, Delhi High Court, 24 July 2026 (§14.1)

legal.title: Commercial entities not automatically excluded from fair dealing
legal.detail: The court rejected the argument that commercial entities are automatically excluded from claiming the fair-dealing defence.
legal.status: prima facie finding at the interim-injunction stage
legal.source: ANI v. OpenAI, Delhi High Court, 24 July 2026 (§14.1)
legal.note: Commentary summarised in the document treats this as one of the ruling's vulnerabilities on appeal — see L08.

legal.title: Practical effect — evidentiary burden shifts to publishers
legal.detail: The burden has shifted onto publishers to prove memorisation or reproduction, not merely ingestion — a considerably harder evidentiary bar. For an India-based project this is a meaningfully favourable environment relative to 12 months ago. "It is not a licence to scrape indiscriminately."
legal.action: Do not read the ruling as permission to scrape; keep the risk-tiered corpus and compliance gate regardless.
legal.source: ANI v. OpenAI, Delhi High Court, 24 July 2026 (§14.1)

legal.title: Limit 1 — these are prima facie findings
legal.detail: The judgment expressly states the findings do not control the final outcome. Discovery, expert evidence and trial are still ahead.
legal.action: Do not architect anything that only works if these findings hold.
legal.source: ANI v. OpenAI, 24 July 2026 — §14.1 "What it does NOT mean" item 1

legal.title: Limit 2 — single-judge interim order, appealable
legal.detail: It is a single-judge interim order; an appellate bench could land differently. Serious commentary has already identified vulnerabilities: that the court treated an internal technical process as "private use" even where the objective purpose is a public commercial product; that it applied Canadian "research" jurisprudence to differently-worded Indian text; and that it arguably used updating construction to create a commercial AI-training exception that Parliament did not enact.
legal.action: Keep the clean tier separable so a compliant base model can be retrained if the ruling is reversed on appeal.
legal.source: ANI v. OpenAI, 24 July 2026 — §14.1 "What it does NOT mean" item 2; mitigation in §18.2
legal.note: The document names no commentator or publication for the "serious commentary".

legal.title: Limit 3 — the hallucination / false-attribution claim is unresolved
legal.detail: ANI's suit always had two limbs; only the training limb was addressed. The hallucination/false-attribution claim remains unresolved.
legal.source: ANI v. OpenAI, 24 July 2026 — §14.1 "What it does NOT mean" item 3
legal.note: This is item 3 of the document's own five-item list. The document does not state which regime the false-attribution limb sounds in (passing off, defamation, or otherwise).

legal.title: Limit 4 — it does not override contracts
legal.detail: A NonCommercial licence (NCERT, DIKSHA, NPTEL) is a contract, not a copyright default. Fair dealing does not let you ignore it.
legal.action: Exclude NC-licensed corpora from a commercial model, or licence them — see L31 and L28.
legal.source: ANI v. OpenAI, 24 July 2026 — §14.1 "What it does NOT mean" item 4

legal.title: Limit 5 — it does not touch the DPDP Act
legal.detail: Copyright and data protection are separate regimes; the ruling says nothing about DPDP obligations.
legal.action: Run the DPDP compliance programme independently of any copyright analysis.
legal.source: ANI v. OpenAI, 24 July 2026 — §14.1 "What it does NOT mean" item 5
legal.note: §14.2 adds that for an India-based training run "data protection is a bigger operational constraint than copyright".

legal.title: India has no explicit TDM exception — the statute was stretched
legal.detail: Unlike the EU (DSM Directive Arts. 3–4) or Japan (Art. 30-4), Indian copyright law is right-holder-centric with a closed list of fair-dealing purposes. The ANI ruling stretched Section 52(1)(a)(i) to cover training. "That stretch is the entire legal foundation, and it is one appeal away from re-examination."
legal.status: no statutory TDM exception; judicial stretch only
legal.action: Assume the foundation can move; keep the corpus decomposable and the clean tier trainable on its own.
legal.source: §14.1, closing paragraph (Copyright Act 1957 s.52(1)(a)(i); EU DSM Directive Arts. 3–4; Japan Art. 30-4)
legal.note: This point sits in its own paragraph in §14.1, outside the numbered five-item "What it does NOT mean" list — so the document actually states six distinct limits on the ruling, not five.

legal.title: You are a Data Fiduciary
legal.detail: You determine the purpose and means of processing training data, so you are a Data Fiduciary. Obligations attach even when data comes from third parties or is processed on external infrastructure.
legal.action: Accept Data Fiduciary duties for the whole pipeline, including third-party corpora and external compute.
legal.source: DPDP Act 2023 + DPDP Rules 2025 (§14.2)
legal.note: §14.2 frames the whole regime: "For an India-based training run, data protection is a bigger operational constraint than copyright."

legal.title: Consent-centric processing
legal.detail: Free, specific, informed consent per specified purpose; notices must itemise the personal data collected and the exact purpose.
legal.action: Itemise personal data and purpose in the notice; do not rely on generic blanket consent.
legal.source: DPDP Act 2023 + DPDP Rules 2025 (§14.2)
legal.note: The document does not state how consent is to be obtained for web-scraped personal data — that gap is what makes the "publicly available" exemption (L16) load-bearing.

legal.title: Erasure obligation — implies selective removal and arguably unlearning
legal.detail: Data must be erased when consent is withdrawn or the purpose is served. This implies the ability to selectively remove data from training pipelines and logs — and, arguably, to handle machine unlearning. Requests must be addressed within 90 days.
legal.action: Build an erasure-request index (document hash → shard → checkpoint lineage) on day one; retrofitting provenance into a 15T-token corpus is effectively impossible.
legal.source: DPDP Act 2023; 90-day deadline at Rule 14, DPDP Rules 2025 (§14.2)
legal.note: The document says machine unlearning is "arguably" required — it does not claim the Act or Rules mandate it expressly.

legal.title: "Publicly available" exemption — scope contested
legal.detail: Section 3(c)(ii) excludes personal data the data principal made publicly available, but the scope is contested. MeitY stated in the Rajya Sabha (Aug 2024) that scraping publicly available user data remains subject to the IT Act, IT Rules and DPDP Act including consent and transparency obligations — which "sits uneasily with the plain text". IAMAI formally petitioned MeitY in August 2025 seeking an explicit AI-training exemption under Section 17(5). As of this writing, no such blanket exemption has been notified.
legal.status: contested — no exemption notified as of 28 July 2026
legal.action: Do not treat "it was public" as a complete answer; keep consent and transparency obligations live for scraped personal data.
legal.source: DPDP Act 2023 s.3(c)(ii); MeitY statement in the Rajya Sabha, Aug 2024; IAMAI petition to MeitY, Aug 2025 seeking s.17(5) exemption (§14.2)

legal.title: Research exemption is purpose-based and may not cover commercial training
legal.detail: Section 17(2)(b) conditionally exempts research processing — but exemptions are purpose-based, and commercial model training is not obviously research.
legal.action: Do not plan on the research exemption for a commercial training run.
legal.note: Recorded as a limit rather than an obligation: it constrains a defence, it does not impose a duty. Note the tension with the copyright side, where the ANI ruling accepted training as "research" under the Copyright Act (L02) — the document does not reconcile the two.

legal.title: Children's data — verifiable parental consent, no profiling
legal.detail: Verifiable parental consent is required for under-18s; no tracking, profiling, or behavioural targeting of children. "For a model trained on educational content this is directly relevant."
legal.action: Add children's-data detection and exclusion to the ingestion gate.
legal.source: DPDP Act 2023 s.9 / Rule 10, DPDP Rules 2025 (§14.2)

legal.title: Cross-border transfer restricted to notified countries
legal.detail: Transfers are permitted to notified countries. Relevant if you train on non-Indian cloud.
legal.action: Check the notified-country list before choosing non-Indian training infrastructure.
legal.source: DPDP Act 2023 s.16 / Rule 15, DPDP Rules 2025 (§14.2)
legal.note: The document does not say which countries are notified.

legal.title: Ingestion gate — PII and India-specific ID detection
legal.detail: The ingestion gate must do PII detection and redaction (names, phones, emails, addresses), India-specific ID pattern detection (Aadhaar, PAN, passport, voter ID, bank), and children's-data detection and exclusion.
legal.action: Build automated Aadhaar/PAN/passport-pattern detectors into ingestion; redact PII and exclude children's data before anything reaches the corpus.
legal.source: §14.2 "Operational requirements this imposes on your pipeline"; §13.4 ("Any government/personal/financial identity documents"); §17 SAFETY & COMPLIANCE GATE
legal.note: The §17 pipeline diagram restates the same gate: "PII redaction · Aadhaar/PAN/passport/bank pattern detection", CSAM hash matching, toxicity, children's-data exclusion, licence tag propagation.

legal.title: Provenance record per document
legal.detail: Keep a provenance record for every document: source URL, licence, retrieval date, hash.
legal.action: Emit a per-document provenance record at ingestion; do not defer it.
legal.source: §14.2 operational-requirements block; §17 SAFETY & COMPLIANCE GATE

legal.title: Erasure-request index (hash → shard → checkpoint lineage)
legal.detail: Maintain an erasure-request index mapping document hash → shard → checkpoint lineage. "The erasure-request index is the part teams skip and later regret. Build it on day one; retrofitting provenance into a 15T-token corpus is effectively impossible."
legal.action: Build the index before the first large ingestion run.
legal.source: §14.2 operational-requirements block; mitigation repeated in §18.2 ("DPDP erasure request against training data")

legal.title: Posture 1 — tier the corpus by risk and prove the clean tier first
legal.detail: Tier your corpus by risk exactly as this document does: build the clean tier first and prove the model works on it.
legal.action: Build and validate on the clean tier before touching restricted material.
legal.source: §14.3 "A defensible legal posture (not legal advice)", item 1

legal.title: Posture 2 — honour robots.txt, noai/noimageai, and TDM reservation signals
legal.detail: Honour robots.txt, `noai`/`noimageai` meta tags, and TDM reservation signals. "Even without a statutory obligation, ignoring them converts an arguable case into a wilful one."
legal.action: Enforce the signals at fetch time in the acquisition stage.
legal.source: §14.3 item 2; restated in the §17 ACQUISITION block ("robots.txt + noai + TDM-reservation honoured at fetch time")

legal.title: Posture 3 — publish a data statement
legal.detail: Publish a data statement covering sources, licences, filtering, and an opt-out mechanism. Dolma and Common Corpus are the models to copy. "Transparency is a legal asset, not a liability."
legal.action: Publish the data statement alongside the model.
legal.source: §14.3 item 3

legal.title: Posture 4 — run and document memorisation testing
legal.detail: Run and document memorisation testing. The ANI ruling turned on ANI's failure to prove memorisation, so being able to affirmatively demonstrate low memorisation "is now a defensive asset with judicial backing".
legal.status: recommended — now an affirmative legal asset in India
legal.action: Run memorisation tests and publish the results.
legal.source: §14.3 item 4; repeated as the §18.2 mitigation for "Model memorises and regurgitates Indic news"

legal.title: Posture 5 — maintain a takedown/opt-out channel and act on it
legal.detail: Maintain a takedown/opt-out channel and act on it.
legal.action: Stand up the channel and process requests.
legal.source: §14.3 item 5
legal.note: The document gives no SLA for this channel; the only stated deadline is the 90-day DPDP erasure window in L15.

legal.title: Posture 6 — get NCERT/MoE and BharatGen licences in writing
legal.detail: Get NCERT/MoE and BharatGen licences in writing. "Two letters could be worth more than a trillion scraped tokens."
legal.action: Pursue written licences from NCERT/MoE and BharatGen.
legal.source: §14.3 item 6
legal.note: §13.2 adds the specific asks: an MoU for Bharat Data Sagar, and the exact EKA licence string in writing.

legal.title: Keep the clean tier separable against an appeal reversal
legal.detail: Mitigation for the risk "ANI ruling reversed on appeal": keep the clean tier separable so you can retrain a compliant base if needed. "Do not architect a corpus you cannot decompose."
legal.action: Keep the corpus decomposable by licence/risk tier so a compliant base can be retrained.
legal.source: §18.2 Legal and reputational risks

legal.title: Hard-fail the build on any NonCommercial licence tag
legal.detail: Mitigation for "NC-licensed content leaks into the mix": automated licence-tag propagation, and hard-fail the build on any NC tag, not a warning.
legal.action: Propagate licence tags through the pipeline and fail the build (not warn) on any NC tag.
legal.source: §18.2 Legal and reputational risks
legal.note: §18.2 adds a related supply-chain rule for synthetic data: prefer Apache-2.0 generators (Qwen3, some Nemotron) for anything that will be redistributed, to avoid Gemma/Llama/Qwen licence-chain terms.

legal.title: NonCommercial-licensed datasets — exclude from a commercial model
legal.detail: Named NC datasets: NCERT textbooks / DIKSHA textbook content (CC BY-NC-ND, NCERT/MoE, K-12 curriculum in 36 languages — NC and ND); DIKSHA non-textbook resources (CC BY-NC-SA); NPTEL / SWAYAM course content (typically CC BY-NC-SA, MoE/IITs/IISc, 2,500+ courses); AI4Bharat IndicNLP Corpus v1 (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, 2.7B words, 10 languages — IndicCorp v2 and Sangraha are NOT NC, only v1 is); NLLB mined bitext (CC BY-NC, Meta); ILDC Indian Legal Documents Corpus (research/non-commercial by request, Malik et al., 35K SC cases); xLAM some releases (CC BY-NC, Salesforce).
legal.status: in force — exclusion or licence required
legal.action: Exclude from a commercial model unless licensed; verify the specific xLAM release before use.
legal.source: §13.1 ("Everything in this section requires either a licence, a legal sign-off, or exclusion")
legal.note: §A.7 confirms NCERT CC BY-NC-ND and DIKSHA CC BY-NC-SA from NCERT/CIET's own site (high confidence). L10 explains why the ANI ruling does not help here.

legal.title: BharatGen non-commercial model licence blocks distillation
legal.detail: BharatGen Param-2 / Patram post-trained checkpoints carry a BharatGen non-commercial licence. These are models, not data — but the licence blocks distillation-based data generation.
legal.action: Do not generate training data by distilling BharatGen checkpoints without a licence.

legal.title: Bespoke / custom licences requiring negotiation
legal.detail: BhashaKritika, 540B synthetic Indic tokens, Krutrim Community License (Krutrim AI Labs / Ola) — negotiate or replicate. Chitrakshara-IL / Chitrakshara-Cap, Krutrim licence — the largest Indic interleaved multimodal corpus. Bharat Data Sagar (BharatGen consortium) — not distributed; pursue an MoU; ₹1,293 crore of public investment, ~20T tokens claimed.
legal.action: Negotiate, replicate, or pursue an MoU before planning around any of these.
legal.note: §18.3 flags the 20T Bharat Data Sagar figure as unaudited; §A.7 grades it low confidence — "a CEO statement... Do not build a plan that depends on this being true."

legal.title: The Stack v2 — OpenRAIL-M, per-file licences, and a live opt-out list
legal.detail: The Stack v2 / StarCoder2 (BigCode / Software Heritage) is under BigCode OpenRAIL-M v1 plus per-file licences plus a live opt-out list.
legal.action: Ingest the opt-out list and use the permissive-only subset.
legal.note: The opt-out list is live, so it must be re-ingested, not snapshotted once — the document says "ingest the opt-out list" without stating a refresh cadence.

legal.title: AIKosh — per-dataset licence ingestion required
legal.detail: AIKosh datasets carry per-dataset licences: open, registered, or restricted, from various contributors via IndiaAI.
legal.action: Ingest and enforce the licence per dataset rather than treating AIKosh as one licence.

legal.title: ULCA / Bhashini — record-level attribution
legal.detail: ULCA / Bhashini datasets are licensed per contributor with record-level attribution (Bhashini DIBD, MeitY).
legal.action: Maintain an attribution manifest at record level.

legal.title: EKA Pre-training Indic Corpus v1 — licence string unspecified
legal.detail: The EKA Pre-training Indic Corpus v1 (Soket AI Labs + IIT Gandhinagar) is described only as "Open Source" — the licence string is unspecified.
legal.action: Get the exact licence in writing before ingesting.
legal.source: §13.2; repeated in §18.3 Honest unknowns ("EKA corpus licence string is unspecified. Get it in writing.")

legal.title: Share-alike (copyleft) sources — attribution plus share-alike
legal.detail: Wikipedia / Wikisource / Wikibooks / FineWiki (CC BY-SA), FLORES-200 (CC BY-SA 4.0) and People's Speech (CC BY-SA) are usable but carry attribution and share-alike obligations.
legal.action: Attribute, and document your share-alike position.

legal.title: Whether model weights are a derivative work of CC BY-SA data is unresolved
legal.detail: Whether model weights are a "derivative work" of CC BY-SA training data is legally unresolved. "Most labs proceed; document your position."
legal.action: Take and document an explicit position rather than leaving it implicit.
legal.source: §13.3; §18.3 Honest unknowns ("unresolved anywhere in the world")

legal.title: Stack Exchange / Stack Overflow — free bulk use is contested
legal.detail: Stack Exchange / Stack Overflow dumps are CC BY-SA, but Stack Overflow now licenses data commercially to AI firms, so free bulk use is contested.
legal.note: The document says "contested" without stating who is asserting what, or whether the CC BY-SA dump licence has actually been withdrawn.

legal.title: Common Crawl carries third-party copyrighted content
legal.detail: Common Crawl WET/WARC is distributed under CC BY (Common Crawl's own terms) but contains third-party copyrighted content. "The fair-dealing question in §14 lives here."
legal.status: in force — the exposure the ANI ruling addresses
legal.note: This is the direct link between the §13 corpus list and the §14 fair-dealing analysis: the CC licence covers the packaging, not the underlying pages.

legal.title: Absolute blocklist — pirated and litigation-tainted book corpora
legal.detail: Books3: pirated books via the Bibliotek torrent, core to Kadrey v. Meta; the original Pile download URL has been dead since ~Sept 2023. LibGen / Library Genesis: pirated, central to Tremblay v. OpenAI allegations. Anna's Archive / Z-Library: pirated shadow libraries.
legal.action: Never ingest these; if you ingest The Pile, strip Books3 first.
legal.source: §13.4 (cases named: Kadrey v. Meta; Tremblay v. OpenAI)
legal.note: The document names these two US cases only as context for why the datasets are tainted; it states no holding, court, or date for either.

legal.title: LAION-5B — CSAM; use Re-LAION-5B only
legal.detail: CSAM was found in the original LAION-5B dataset (Thiel, Dec 2023) and it was taken down from hosting services; documented PII/medical-record leakage as well.
legal.action: Use Re-LAION-5B (Aug 2024) only, and even then with a fresh safety scan; run PhotoDNA-equivalent hash matching on every image.
legal.source: §13.4 (Thiel, Dec 2023); CSAM hash-matching mitigation in §18.2 and §17
legal.note: Regime left null: the document grounds this in child-safety plus documented PII leakage rather than a named statute.

legal.title: DataComp CommonPool — documented large-scale privacy problems
legal.detail: DataComp CommonPool has documented large-scale privacy problems (arXiv:2506.17185) and substantial overlap with LAION-5B.
legal.action: Avoid, or apply your own PII/CSAM filtering pipeline first.

legal.title: WebVid-10M — withdrawn by its creators
legal.detail: WebVid-10M was withdrawn by its creators.
legal.action: Do not use.
legal.note: The document does not state the reason for the withdrawal.

legal.title: OpenSubtitles — copyrighted film/TV subtitles inside OPUS
legal.detail: OpenSubtitles, distributed within OPUS, is copyrighted film/TV subtitle text.
legal.action: Filter it explicitly out of any OPUS ingestion.
legal.source: §13.4; also flagged in the §7 OPUS row
legal.note: Note the tension the document itself surfaces: §A.4's conversational IndicTrans2 adaptation (arXiv:2606.29024) achieves its result using OpenSubtitles among its "only public data".

legal.title: Alpaca-lineage data — OpenAI ToS provenance taint
legal.detail: Alpaca, Bactrian-X, mAlpaca and many "self-instruct" sets were generated with OpenAI models, and OpenAI's ToS prohibits using outputs to train competing models. "Materially risky for a model that will compete with OpenAI."
legal.action: Prefer Aya, Tülu 3, Nemotron, OpenThoughts, UPDESH instead.
legal.source: §13.4; cross-referenced at §11.1 (Bactrian-X)

legal.title: Reddit / Pushshift — licence or skip
legal.detail: Reddit now licenses data commercially (~$203M disclosed contract value at IPO; ~$60M/yr Google, ~$70M/yr OpenAI reported). Free bulk scraping is against ToS and actively enforced.
legal.action: Do not scrape. License or skip.
legal.source: §13.4; deal figures repeated in §15.2 (all figures "reported", not confirmed by parties)

legal.title: Twitter/X archives — ToS and active enforcement
legal.detail: Twitter/X archives are covered by ToS restrictions with active enforcement.
legal.action: Skip.

legal.title: YouTube-derived corpora — ToS prohibits bulk download
legal.detail: YouTube-Commons, YODAS, Panda-70M, InternVid and HD-VILA are YouTube-derived; YouTube ToS prohibits bulk download regardless of the underlying CC licence on individual videos.
legal.action: Document a position or skip.
legal.source: §13.4; also flagged in §9.2

legal.title: Scraped Indian news — where the risk concentrates
legal.detail: "The ANI v. OpenAI litigation exists precisely because of this." The Digital News Publishers Association and the Federation of Indian Publishers are intervenors. The legal position improved dramatically in July 2026, "but this is where the risk concentrates".
legal.action: For Indian news, negotiate a retrieval/grounding deal rather than a training deal — cheaper, more readily accepted by publishers, and for a conversational model it delivers most of the value.
legal.source: §13.4; the retrieval-not-training recommendation is from §15.3
legal.note: §15.3 grounds that recommendation in the market shift to live-access deals (2 in 2023 → 11 in 2024 → 18 in 2025 → ~34 projected in 2026), with the Washington Post/OpenAI (April 2025) and Le Monde/Perplexity deals explicitly excluding training.

legal.title: Identity documents — absolute blocklist
legal.detail: Any government, personal or financial identity documents are barred under the DPDP Act "and also basic ethics".
legal.action: Build automated Aadhaar/PAN/passport-pattern detectors into ingestion.
legal.note: Same control as L20; recorded separately because §13.4 states it as a corpus-level prohibition rather than a pipeline requirement.

legal.title: Internet Archive Indian book scans — item-level rights clearance
legal.detail: The Internet Archive's Public Library of India / Digital Library of India holds ~500K+ scanned Indian books of mixed copyright status, many still in copyright. "Requires item-level rights clearance. Enormous prize, real risk."
legal.action: Clear rights item by item before ingesting.
legal.source: §10.2 clean curriculum sources table
legal.note: Outside §§13–14, but recorded here because it is a licensing constraint of the same class. Related: §10.2 notes Shodhganga (INFLIBNET) Indian PhD theses retain author copyright per thesis.

trends.trend: The market shifted from 'training' to 'live access'. Attribution/live-access deals went 2 (2023) -> 11 (2024) -> 18 (2025) -> ~34 projected (2026), and deals such as The Washington Post's April 2025 OpenAI deal and Le Monde's Perplexity deal explicitly exclude training — content can be surfaced and attributed but not learned.
trends.implication: For Indian news, negotiate a retrieval/grounding deal rather than a training deal. It is far cheaper, publishers accept it more readily, and for a conversational model it delivers most of the value.

trends.trend: No single publisher has dominant leverage. Even the largest sellers have single-digit deal counts (Shutterstock 7, Wikimedia 6, Reddit 5), while 'other' publishers collectively account for 36 deals.
trends.implication: You do not need Times of India — you need forty regional-language publishers, each with very little individual leverage and considerable incentive. The Indian regional press (Dainik Jagran, Malayala Manorama, Eenadu, Daily Thanthi, Sakal, Anandabazar Patrika and the hundreds beneath them) is exactly the fragmented, monetisation-hungry, linguistically-irreplaceable long tail this pattern predicts you can afford.

trends.trend: The total market is small relative to compute: AI training-data licensing is estimated at ~$4B globally in 2026.
trends.implication: Against a 300B-model training budget, a Rs 5-20 crore ($600K-$2.4M) Indic content licensing programme is a rounding error that buys the one thing money can buy in this project: exclusive, high-quality, natural Indic text that no competitor has.
